result: Multiple sequence alignment of characterized AA11 PMOs reveals that three of four maintain a three-part architecture (PMO domain, GS-rich linker, X278 domain), while one is a single-domain PMO. All AA11 proteins contain a signal peptide that is cleaved to leave an N-terminal histidine.
evaluation: Claims C67-C70 are supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing the MSA and domain architecture. The structural characterization is consistent with known AA11 family properties and provides clear evidence for the domain organization.

result: The PMO domain alone of CWR-1 is sufficient to confer the allorecognition checkpoint and block cell fusion. Truncated versions lacking the GS linker and/or X278 domain still block fusion with incompatible cwr-2 strains but fuse normally with permissive mutants.
evaluation: Claims C71-C73 and C9 are strongly supported by Figure 1B-C showing fusion blockage with all truncation constructs when paired with incompatible cwr-2HG3, and Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-D showing normal fusion with permissive mutants. Statistical significance is demonstrated with appropriate controls.

result: CWR-1HG1 PMO domain is confirmed as a C1-oxidizing chitin PMO. It binds ~0.7 equivalents of copper, reduces oxygen to hydrogen peroxide in the presence of ascorbate, and generates C1-oxidized products from β-chitin. MS/MS analysis confirms C1 regioselectivity.
evaluation: Claims C75-C81 and C8 are well-supported by Figure 1E showing copper binding, oxygen reduction, and HPAEC-PAD traces with C1-oxidized products. Figure 1—figure supplement 5 provides standards, and Figure 1—figure supplement 6 shows MS/MS confirmation. The data are consistent with characterized AA11 PMOs.

result: Phylogenetic and sequence analysis of CWR-1 PMO domains from six haplogroups shows >95% intra-haplogroup identity, conservation of catalytic residues, and inter-haplogroup differences concentrated in LC, LS, and L2 loops known to affect substrate binding and specificity.
evaluation: Claims C82-C88 are supported by Figure 2A (phylogenetic tree), Figure 2B (sequence alignment), Figure 2C (homology models), and Supplementary file 1e. The identification of variable loops is consistent with known PMO structure-function relationships (C85-C86 with citations).

result: Full-length and chimeric cwr-1 constructs containing PMO domains from different haplogroups block fusion with incompatible cwr-2 strains but fuse normally with permissive mutants. The PMO domain alone confers allorecognition specificity in trans.
evaluation: Claims C89-C95 are supported by Figure 3A-F showing fusion blockage with all haplogroup PMO domains and chimeras when paired with incompatible cwr-2, and normal fusion with permissive controls. Statistical analysis with appropriate replicates is provided. The trans-acting mechanism is demonstrated by the experimental design.

result: All six CWR-1 PMO proteins from different haplogroups exhibit similar biochemical properties: they oxidatively degrade α- and β-chitin (with β-chitin more efficiently), generate C1-oxidized products, bind ~1 equivalent of copper, and reduce oxygen at similar rates. No activity was observed on other substrates tested.
evaluation: Claims C96-C101, C132-C133 are supported by Figure 4A-D showing HPAEC-PAD traces, copper stoichiometry, and oxygen reduction assays for all six haplogroups. Supplementary file 1f documents lack of activity on other substrates. The data demonstrate functional conservation despite sequence differences.

result: PMO reaction products from CWR-1HG1 and CWR-1HG4 on chitin and purified cell walls do not block or reduce cell fusion frequencies between compatible strains.
evaluation: Claim C102 is supported by Figure 4—figure supplement 1 showing that addition of PMO reaction products or cell walls from incompatible strains does not affect fusion between compatible strains. This rules out a product-based signaling mechanism.

result: Histidine-brace mutants of CWR-1 PMO are catalytically inactive on β-chitin. Single His→Ala mutants retain copper binding and oxygen reduction activity (though reduced), while double mutants greatly reduce both. EPR analysis shows the H78A mutation significantly alters the Cu(II) coordination environment.
evaluation: Claims C104-C109 are supported by Figure 5A-D showing loss of chitin-degrading activity, copper binding data, oxygen reduction assays, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2 showing EPR spectra. The biochemical characterization is thorough and consistent with known PMO active site requirements.

result: Catalytically inactive histidine-brace mutants (H20A, H78A, H20A;H78A) and tyrosine mutant (Y159A) of CWR-1 still trigger allorecognition and block cell fusion with incompatible cwr-2 strains, ruling out enzymatic activity and H2O2 generation as factors in the fusion checkpoint.
evaluation: Claims C110-C116, C10, C128 are strongly supported by Figure 5E-F showing fusion blockage with all catalytically inactive mutants when paired with incompatible cwr-2HG3, and normal fusion with compatible controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C-D). This is a critical finding demonstrating a moonlighting function independent of catalytic activity.

result: A chimera swapping only the LS loop (V86-T130) maintains HG1 specificity, but a larger chimera (V86-D202 encompassing LS, L8, and LC loops) exhibits novel specificity with partial compatibility to multiple haplogroups, particularly HG4 and HG6, but not full compatibility with any.
evaluation: Claims C117-C123, C11-C12 are supported by Figure 6B-E showing fusion percentages of chimeric constructs with different cwr-2 haplogroups. The data demonstrate that the V86-D202 region contains some but not all determinants of specificity, creating a novel recognition pattern. Statistical analysis is provided.

result: The N. crassa cell wall remodeling checkpoint acts in trans via nonenzymatic interactions between CWR-1 and CWR-2. The PMO domain alone confers allelic specificity, likely through protein-protein interactions, with contact points potentially extending beyond the LS, LC, and L8 regions.
evaluation: Claims C124-C130, C13 represent the main conclusions supported by the collective experimental evidence: domain truncations (C71-C73), catalytically inactive mutants (C112), chimera experiments (C117-C123), and trans-acting design (C89-C95). The interpretation is well-justified by the data.

result: Aspects associated with cell wall dissolution, including vesicle delivery or activation of cell wall remodeling enzymes, could potentially be targets of CWR-1/CWR-2 interactions.
evaluation: Claim C131 is stated as a hypothesis in the Discussion without experimental support. While plausible given the fusion blockage phenotype, no direct evidence for the mechanism of how CWR-1/CWR-2 interactions block fusion is provided. This represents speculation about future work.

result: The activity of the CWR-1 PMO domain is similar to characterized single-domain AA11 PMOs, suggesting that the two AA11 architectures (with and without GS linker/X278 domain) may be functionally redundant for chitin degradation.
evaluation: Claims C134-C135 are supported by comparison of CWR-1 PMO activity data (Figure 4) with cited literature on single-domain AA11 PMOs. The interpretation is reasonable given the similar C1-oxidative activity on chitin substrates, though the redundancy claim is somewhat speculative.

result: The GS linker and X278 domain may allow CWR-1 to remain bound to the cell wall through chitin-protein interactions, potentially aiding in cell wall dissolution. The Δcwr-1Δ81Δcwr-2 mutant shows a slight delay in fusion between compatible cells, consistent with this hypothesis.
evaluation: Claims C136-C138 are partially supported. C138 is supported by citation to prior work (Gonçalves et al., 2019). C136-C137 represent reasonable speculation based on the domain architecture and PMO activity data, though direct evidence for the proposed chitin-binding function of X278 is not provided in this study.

result: Discussion of PMO active site requirements and potential in vivo effects of histidine-brace mutants, including speculation about aromatic residue requirements, H2O2 generation, and effects on protein stability.
evaluation: Claims C139-C143 are primarily speculative interpretations in the Discussion. C139-C140 are supported by citations to prior work. C141-C142 are speculations about mechanisms. C143 interprets the increased fusion percentages (~20% vs ~6%) with mutants as potentially indicating stability or conformational changes, but this is not directly tested.

result: The region of the PMO domain essential for allelic specificity encompasses additional residues beyond the chimeric-loop constructs tested. The cwr-1HG1/HG6 chimera may confer a novel specificity and will be useful for future studies defining CWR-2 specificity determinants.
evaluation: Claims C144-C147 are reasonable interpretations of the chimera data (C117-C123). C144 is supported by the incomplete specificity switch. C145 is speculation about requirements. C146 is supported by the novel fusion pattern. C147 represents proposed future work, which is appropriate for Discussion.

result: The data highlight a moonlighting role of the CWR-1 PMO domain in allorecognition, distinct from its catalytic function. This is compared to other moonlighting proteins and distinguished from the P. aeruginosa CopD PMO where catalytic activity is required for immune evasion.
evaluation: Claims C14, C149-C154 represent the main conclusion and contextualization. C14 is well-supported by the collective evidence showing catalytically inactive mutants retain allorecognition function. C149-C153 provide appropriate context through citations. C154 is reasonable speculation based on sequence similarity (Figure 1—figure supplements 1-2).

result: cwr-1 transcripts are upregulated during starvation and fruiting body development, suggesting dual biological roles. Allorecognition loci in filamentous fungi are under balancing selection, and linked cwr-1/cwr-2 loci with haplogroups are found in several other fungal species.
evaluation: Claims C155-C158 are supported by citations to prior work (RNA-seq data, population genetics studies). These provide important biological context for the moonlighting function and evolutionary significance of the cwr system.

result: Background on N. crassa allorecognition system: three cell fusion checkpoints control mycelial network formation. The cwr locus (encoding cwr-1 and cwr-2) controls the second checkpoint for cell wall dissolution. Six haplogroups exist with allelic specificity determining fusion compatibility.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6, C33-C47 provide essential background information supported by citations to prior work. These establish the biological context and prior knowledge foundation for the current study. The claims are well-documented in the literature.

result: Background on PMOs: they are auxiliary redox enzymes that degrade various polysaccharides, have industrial applications, and play diverse biological roles. All PMOs contain a signal peptide and N-terminal histidine that binds copper. AA11 family members show chitin-degradation activity.
evaluation: Claims C7, C48-C66 provide comprehensive background on PMO biology and biochemistry, all supported by appropriate citations. C65-C66 include some speculation about the X278 domain function based on structural analysis, which is reasonable given the context.

result: Background on allorecognition across biology: various organisms use allorecognition systems to distinguish self from non-self, including social amoebae, bacteria, plants, invertebrates, and vertebrates (MHC). In filamentous fungi, allorecognition regulates the interconnected hyphal network and prevents exploitation.
evaluation: Claims C15-C32 provide broad biological context for allorecognition, all supported by appropriate citations. This establishes the significance of studying allorecognition mechanisms and places the fungal system in comparative context.
